newsitem.title: USA: California lawmen plot response to marijuana law.
newsitem.headline: California lawmen plot response to marijuana law.

text.p: California Attorney General Dan Lungren said Tuesday that a controversial state measure legalising marijuana use by sick people should be interpreted as narrowly as possible by law enforcement.

Lungren spoke after meeting in Sacramento with the state's police chiefs, sheriffs and district attorneys to discuss an initiative passed by California voters Nov. 5 which allows sick people to legally possess and grow marijuana for medical use when recommended by a doctor.
The state measure, Proposition 215, clashes with federal law, which states that marijuana is an illegal drug and that doctors may be prosecuted for prescribing it.

"Our job is to correctly apply the 'medicinal use' law as narrowly as possible -- as close as possible to what the voters' intentions were," Lungren said. "Law enforcement's job is to also ensure this law is not abused by people who want to smoke marijuana for other than 'legitimate medicinal purposes.'"
Lungren said marijuana could not be used to treat minor ailments such as acne, stress or arthritis. "The passage of Proposition 215 is not tantamount to legalising marijuana," he said.

He advised the officials that a doctor must recommend marijuana for a patient and not just rubber stamp its use. The doctor should find that the benefits of marijuana use for that patient clearly outweighed the risks -- a finding that Lungren said was "believed to be scientifically unsupportable."
Lungren, a Republican who takes a hard line on law and order, is one of many officials in state and federal government who strongly opposed Proposition 215.

Voter approval of medical marijuana measures in California and Arizona has caused alarm in Washington. At a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in Washington Monday, Republican senators suggested stepping up enforcement of federal anti-drug laws to blunt the effect of the two state measures.

Supporters of Proposition 215 say marijuana often eases nausea in cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, reduces the pain of AIDS patients and lowers eye pressure in glaucoma sufferers. But opponents alleged the measure was an attempt to legalise marijuana through the back door and said it was so loosely worded that an upset stomach or a stiff neck could be cited as reasons for its use.
Lungren said his office was in contact with federal officials to try to clarify the conflicting state and federal laws and the federal government's enforcement and prosecution plans.

Since the California law was passed by the voters, it cannot be changed except by another vote of the people, Lungren said. However, he said, the state legislature may enact statutes to regulate the law's implementation, such as banning bus drivers from driving when under the influence of marijuana.
Lungren's office said he would raise the medical marijuana issue at a meeting in Washington next week with U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno.
